title: RV Park Investing Returns and Cap Rates: What Investors Need to Know in 2024
excerpt: RV park investing offers some of the strongest cap rates in commercial real estate, often ranging from 7% to 12%. Learn how to evaluate returns, calculate cap rates, and find profitable RV park deals in today's market.

sections.content: RV park investing has moved from a niche strategy to a mainstream asset class. Institutional investors, family offices, and individual investors are all buying into campgrounds and RV parks at record rates. The reason is simple: the numbers work. RV park investing returns and cap rates consistently outperform many traditional real estate asset classes, often delivering cap rates between 7% and 12% — sometimes higher in secondary markets. If you are looking to diversify beyond single-family homes or apartments, understanding how RV park returns stack up could open a profitable new door.
Why RV Parks Are Attracting Serious Investors

The RV industry boomed during and after the pandemic. Roughly 11.2 million U.S. households now own an RV, according to the RV Industry Association — an all-time high. RV parks benefited directly from this surge. Occupancy rates climbed, nightly rates jumped, and owners who had operated mom-and-pop parks for decades suddenly found institutional buyers knocking on their doors. For investors, this created a rare window: an asset class with strong demand fundamentals, relatively low operational complexity compared to hotels, and cap rates that still reflect the market's slower adoption of the space.

RV parks are the last great fragmented real estate sector. Thousands of underperforming, family-owned parks sit ripe for professional management and modest capital improvements — and the returns reflect that opportunity.
Understanding Cap Rates in RV Park Investing

A cap rate (capitalization rate) is one of the most important metrics in commercial real estate. It measures a property's income relative to its purchase price. The formula is straightforward: divide the Net Operating Income (NOI) by the property's market value or purchase price. A park generating $150,000 in NOI purchased for $1,500,000 has a 10% cap rate. For deeper reading on how this formula applies across asset types, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners).
Typical Cap Rates by Market Tier

items: Primary markets (high-traffic tourist destinations): 5% to 7% cap rates — lower due to higher acquisition prices
Secondary markets (regional travel corridors): 7% to 9% cap rates — the sweet spot for most investors
Tertiary or rural markets: 9% to 12%+ cap rates — higher risk, but significant upside for value-add plays
Distressed or mismanaged parks: Cap rates can appear above 12%, but underperforming revenue requires careful due diligence
Luxury glamping resorts: Often priced at 5% to 6% caps due to premium positioning and strong demand

sections.content: Pro Tip: Do not just trust the seller's stated cap rate. Always reconstruct the NOI from raw data. Many RV park sellers use owner-adjusted income figures that inflate NOI. Request 2-3 years of tax returns, utility bills, and reservation software reports to build your own income model. You can run the numbers quickly using our free [Cap Rate Calculator at aiwholesail.com/tools/cap-rate-calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/cap-rate-calculator).
How to Calculate NOI for an RV Park

Net Operating Income is the engine of every cap rate calculation. For RV parks, revenue streams are more diverse than a typical apartment building. A well-run park might collect income from nightly and monthly site fees, dump station fees, laundry machines, camp store sales, firewood bundles, WiFi upgrades, and seasonal site rentals. Operational expenses typically include property taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance, management fees (usually 8-12% of gross revenue), marketing, and reserve contributions. Let's look at a real-world example.
Example: 80-Site RV Park in a Secondary Market

items: Total sites: 80 (60 overnight/transient, 20 monthly long-term)
Average nightly rate: $45 | Average occupancy: 65% for transient sites
Monthly site rent: $450/month average across 20 sites
Annual revenue from transient sites: 60 sites × $45 × 0.65 × 365 = approximately $641,250
Annual revenue from monthly sites: 20 × $450 × 12 = $108,000
Ancillary income (store, laundry, dump station): $22,000
Gross Revenue: approximately $771,250
Operating Expenses (40% expense ratio): approximately $308,500
NOI: approximately $462,750
At a 9% cap rate: Estimated property value of $5.14 million

sections.content: Expense ratios for RV parks typically run between 35% and 50%, which is significantly lower than apartment complexes (which often run 45-55%). This difference in operating efficiency is one reason RV parks deliver competitive cash-on-cash returns even after debt service. If you are new to evaluating commercial deals, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) covers the fundamentals of analyzing income-producing properties from the ground up.
Cash-on-Cash Returns vs. Cap Rates

Cap rate is a property-level metric — it ignores financing. Cash-on-cash return measures what you actually earn on the cash you put in after paying your mortgage. RV park investors using conservative 25-30% down payments and 20-25 year amortization schedules on commercial loans (typically 6-8% interest in today's market) commonly see cash-on-cash returns of 8% to 14% on stabilized parks. Value-add plays — parks where you can raise rates, increase occupancy, or add sites — can push those returns considerably higher in years 2 through 5.
Markets Driving Strong RV Park Returns

Location drives everything in RV park performance. Parks near national parks, interstate highways, lakes, or Sun Belt metros tend to perform best. Growing metros like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) all have strong surrounding RV park demand driven by year-round warm weather, consistent road-trip culture, and millions of visitors. Secondary markets within 2-3 hours of these cities often offer the best combination of high occupancy and double-digit cap rates.
What to Look for in a High-Return RV Park Market

items: Proximity to a major interstate, state park, or tourist attraction within 30 minutes
Year-round or at least 8-month operating season to maximize revenue days
Low local competition — fewer than 3 comparable parks within 25 miles
Strong population growth in the surrounding county (RV ownership scales with housing growth)
Access to municipal water and sewer, or a well-maintained private system (avoids costly utility issues)
Zoning that allows for future expansion or glamping additions

sections.content: Value-Add Strategies That Boost Cap Rates

Many RV parks trade at cap rates that reflect poor management rather than poor location. A park charging $28 per night in a market where competitors charge $45 represents a massive value-add opportunity. Other common improvements include adding pull-through sites for large Class A rigs (which command premium rates), installing upgraded electrical (50-amp hookups vs. 30-amp), building a small camp store, or adding glamping tents or cabins that generate 2-3x the revenue per night of a standard RV site. Even a rate increase of $8 per night across 60 transient sites adds over $100,000 in annual gross revenue — and at a 9% cap rate, that single improvement could add more than $1 million in property value.

Pro Tip: When evaluating a value-add park, calculate the 'forced appreciation' potential before making an offer. Identify two or three specific improvements, estimate the revenue lift, and run the projected NOI through your cap rate model to see the potential jump in property value. This is your negotiating anchor for price.
Risks to Factor Into Your Return Projections

items: Seasonality risk: Many parks earn 70-80% of annual revenue in just 4-5 months — budget conservatively for off-season cash flow
Management intensity: RV parks require active hospitality management; factor in a professional manager at 8-12% of gross revenue if you are not local
Infrastructure costs: Aging septic systems, electrical panels, and road surfaces can cost $50,000-$300,000 to repair or replace
Zoning changes: Some municipalities are restricting new RV parks — verify zoning protection and expansion rights before closing
Environmental concerns: Older parks may have underground storage tanks or septic issues — always get a Phase I environmental assessment

sections.content: RV park investing is not passive by nature, but it can become semi-passive with the right systems and local management team in place. Investors who underwrite conservatively — using 55% to 60% occupancy for transient sites, realistic expense ratios, and current debt costs — tend to outperform expectations rather than fall short. The investors who struggle are those who buy a seller's optimistic projections without building their own income model from scratch.
